title: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
summary: How a model of the key CDF plus error bounds can replace B-tree traversal: the Recursive Model Index, last-mile search, the error-bounded PGM-index, updatable ALEX, and Bigtable in production.
outcomes: Explain why a range index is a model of the key CDF and how min and max error bounds keep lookups exact
Trace a lookup through a 2-stage Recursive Model Index and compute its leaf predictions and search window
Choose between bounded binary search and exponential search, and fix lookups broken by non-monotonic models
Build epsilon-bounded PGM segments by hand and predict how segment count and depth change with epsilon
Decide when a learned index pays off, from read-only arrays to ALEX inserts and LSM or Bigtable files

lessons.title: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits

blocks.md: From the B-tree course you know the job of a range index: given a lookup key, find the first record whose key is equal to or greater than it, so that point lookups and range scans both work. This course looks at that job from a different angle, the one taken by Kraska, Beutel, Chi, Dean and Polyzotis in *The Case for Learned Index Structures* (SIGMOD 2018).

Their setting is deliberately simple: an in-memory, read-only array of records sorted by key, like the dense arrays that cache-optimized in-memory B-trees index. Many B-trees index only the first key of each page. Seen from outside, such a B-tree takes a key and returns a page, which is a **position** with an error between 0 and the page size. The key is guaranteed to be inside that range if it exists. In machine learning words, the B-tree is a regression tree: it maps a key to a position, with a known minimum and maximum error.

blocks.title: Two ways to turn a key into a position

nodes.label:
page:
pos to pos + page size

window:
pos - min_err to pos + max_err

scenes.caption: Both paths end the same way: a short search inside a small range of the sorted array. They differ in how they produce that range.
A B-tree narrows the range with a chain of comparisons, one node per level, and ends at a page. The page is a position estimate whose error is at most the page size.
A learned index replaces the comparisons with arithmetic. A model predicts a position, and stored error bounds say how far off it can be.
Same contract, different machinery: both guarantee the key is inside the final range if it exists. Only the cost and size of producing the range change.

blocks.md: Why is predicting a position a learning problem at all? In a sorted array, the position of key $x$ is the number of keys smaller than $x$. Divide by the number of keys $N$ and you get the fraction of keys below $x$, which is the empirical **cumulative distribution function** (CDF) of the keys. So the paper writes the position estimate as:

blocks.caption: F is a model of the CDF, P(X <= key), and N is the number of keys. Learning an index means learning the distribution of the keys.

blocks.md: If the keys are the integers from 1,000,000 to 1,999,999, a single line predicts every position exactly: one multiply and one add, no matter how many keys there are. A B-tree still pays one node per level. Real keys are not that regular, so a model will be wrong by a few positions. The trick is to measure *how* wrong over the stored keys and remember it.

Here is a tiny example. Ten sorted keys, and a straight line fitted by least squares to the points (key, position). The fitted line is $f(x) = 0.1525x + 0.8403$, and the prediction is $f(x)$ rounded to the nearest position and clamped to the last position, 9 (key 58 gives 9.68, which would otherwise round past the end).

blocks.title: Fitting one line to ten sorted keys

scenes.caption: The data: ten keys in a sorted array. The index above each cell is the true position, which is what the model must predict.
Evaluate the fitted line at every stored key. The values track the positions but drift: the keys bunch up near 3 to 9 and spread out after 26.
Round to the nearest position. Most predictions land exactly; a few are off by one.
Record the error true minus predicted for every key. Over all stored keys the worst under-prediction is -1 and the worst over-prediction is +1, so min_err = -1 and max_err = +1.
Lookup 26: f(26) = 4.80, so the prediction is 5. The window is positions 4 to 6, and a search of just three cells finds 26 at position 6.

blocks.md: A learned range index is a model of the key CDF plus two stored numbers per model, min_err and max_err. The model makes a guess; the error bounds turn the guess into a guarantee for every stored key.

Two details from the paper matter later. First, the error bounds are computed over the stored keys only, which is also true of a B-tree: it, too, must be rebalanced (in ML terms, retrained) when data changes. Second, the bounds are only a convenience. Because the array is sorted, any prediction can be corrected by searching outward from it, which is how later designs drop the stored bounds entirely.
A learned index does not return approximate answers. It finds exactly the same record a B-tree would. Only the *path* to the record is approximate; the final local search makes the answer exact.

blocks.question: Using the same line and bounds (min_err = -1, max_err = +1), you look up key 30, which is not stored. f(30) = 5.41. Which positions do you search, and what lower_bound do you return?
options: Positions 4 to 6; the first key >= 30 is not there, so return not found
Positions 4 to 6; return position 6, the last slot in the window, which holds 26
Only position 5, because the error bound is for stored keys
Positions 4 to 6, then continue right: 41 at position 7 is the lower_bound
blocks.explain: The prediction rounds to 5, so the window is 4 to 6, holding 21, 24 and 26, all smaller than 30. The answer sits just past the window edge at position 7. Bounds measured on stored keys say nothing certain about absent keys, so when the search ends at a window boundary you must extend it. Kraska et al. describe exactly this fix.

blocks.question: A B-tree with pages of 128 keys and a model with min_err = -40, max_err = +60 both index the same array. In terms of the final search, which statement is right?
options: The model is worse because its errors can be negative
Both leave a range of about 100 to 128 slots to search; they are the same kind of object
The B-tree is exact and the model is approximate, so only the model needs a final search
The model needs no final search if its average error is small
blocks.explain: A page is a position estimate with min error 0 and max error 127. The model's range is 101 slots. Both end with a bounded search. That equivalence is the core observation of the paper: a B-tree already is a model with error bounds.

lessons.title: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index

blocks.md: The paper's first attempt was a naive one: a two-layer fully connected network with 32 ReLU units per layer, trained in TensorFlow on 200M web-server log timestamps, called from Python. It ran at about 1,250 predictions per second, roughly 80,000 ns per lookup *before* any search. A B-tree over the same data took about 300 ns, and binary search over the whole array about 900 ns.

blocks.prompt: Invocation overhead was one problem (TensorFlow is built for big models). But suppose you removed it entirely. Why might one neural network still be a poor index for 200M keys?
blocks.reveal: Because of the **last mile**. A CDF looks smooth from far away, so a small model easily narrows 200M positions down to a region of thousands. But zoomed in, the CDF of real keys is irregular at the level of single records. Driving the error from thousands down to hundreds with *one* model takes far more parameters and multiplications. B-trees are good at exactly this part: a few if-statements split the space finely and overfit the data cheaply.

blocks.md: How much arithmetic can a model afford? The paper's back-of-the-envelope: a B-tree over 100M records with 100 keys per page has $\log_{100} 10^8 = 4$ levels, and each node shrinks the search range by a factor of 100. Binary search inside one node costs roughly 50 cycles, and a CPU can issue 8 to 16 SIMD operations per cycle. So a model wins if it achieves a precision gain better than 1/100 per $50 \times 8 = 400$ arithmetic operations, even with every B-tree node already in cache.

The **Recursive Model Index** (RMI) uses this budget well. It is a hierarchy of models in *stages*. Stage 0 is one model that sees every key. Its output does not need to be a good position: it only chooses which model in the next stage to ask. The last stage predicts the position. Each model in the last stage only has to fit a small slice of the keys, which is a much easier last-mile problem.

blocks.tex: L_0 = \sum_{(x,y)} \big(f_0(x) - y\big)^2 \qquad L_\ell = \sum_{(x,y)} \big(f_\ell^{(\lfloor M_\ell f_{\ell-1}(x)/N \rfloor)}(x) - y\big)^2
blocks.caption: Stage-wise training from the paper: x is a key, y its position, M_l the number of models in stage l. Each model is trained on squared error over only the keys routed to it.

blocks.md: Training happens stage by stage, not end to end. Train stage 0 on all keys, run it to route each key to a stage-1 model, train each stage-1 model on its own keys, and so on. Finally, run the last stage on every stored key and store each leaf model's min_err and max_err. There is no search between stages: a model's output is directly turned into the index of the next model.

Now a worked example with 16 skewed keys and a 2-stage RMI: one linear model on top, $M = 4$ linear leaf models below. All lines are least-squares fits; predictions round to the nearest position and are clamped to 0 to 15 (key 120 gives 18.21 under the single line), and leaf numbers are clamped to 0 to 3.

blocks.title: One line versus a 2-stage RMI on 16 skewed keys

scenes.caption: Sixteen keys: dense at the low end (1 to 15), sparse at the high end (55 to 120). The CDF bends, so no single line fits it well.
One line, f0(x) = 0.1215x + 3.6272, fitted to all keys. Errors run from -4 to +2, so every lookup must search a 7-slot window.
Reuse that same line as stage 0, but only to route: leaf = floor(4 x f0(x) / 16). The slices are uneven (2, 9, 2 and 3 keys). Unlike a B-tree, an RMI does not balance its children.
Each leaf fits its own line to its own keys. The errors shrink to the range -1 to +1 (leaf L1) and 0 (the other three). The worst window drops from 7 slots to 3.

blocks.md: The leaf models and their stored bounds are: L0 $(a, b) = (1.0000, -1.0000)$, error 0; L1 $(0.2643, 2.1524)$, errors from -1 to +1; L2 $(0.0714, 8.0714)$, error 0; L3 $(0.0395, 10.3158)$, error 0. Step through a lookup of key 12 below.

blocks.title: Looking up key 12 in the 2-stage RMI
blocks.code:
def lookup(q):
    s1 = a0 * q + b0            # stage 0: rough position
    j = clamp(floor(M * s1 / N), 0, M - 1)
    a, b, lo_err, hi_err = leaves[j]
    p = clamp(round(a * q + b), 0, N - 1)
    lo = max(0, p + lo_err)
    hi = min(N - 1, p + hi_err) + 1   # exclusive
    while lo < hi:                    # lower_bound
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if keys[mid] < q:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

scenes.caption: Stage 0 evaluates its line. 5.085 is a poor position estimate (key 12 is at position 6), but it only has to pick a leaf.
Route without searching: floor(4 x 5.085 / 16) = floor(1.271) = 1, so leaf L1 handles this key.
Leaf L1 predicts 0.2643 x 12 + 2.1524 = 5.324, which rounds to 5.
The stored bounds give a window of positions 4 to 6 (hi = 7 is exclusive). Only 3 of the 16 keys are candidates.
mid = 5 holds key 9, which is smaller than 12, so the answer is to the right: lo becomes 6.
mid = 6 holds key 12, not smaller than 12, so hi becomes 6. The loop ends and lookup returns position 6: two comparisons in total.

blocks.md: An RMI separates model size from execution cost. A lookup evaluates exactly one model per stage, however many leaf models exist. Adding leaves makes each leaf's slice smaller and its error bounds tighter without adding work per lookup.

The paper also builds **hybrid indexes**: after training, any leaf whose maximum absolute error exceeds a threshold is replaced by a small B-tree over its keys. In the worst case, when no model fits, every leaf becomes a B-tree, which bounds the learned index's worst case by a B-tree's. In the reported experiments, small networks (0 to 2 hidden layers) worked best on top and plain linear models at the bottom, since linear models are cheap and can be fitted optimally in one pass.

Do not read stage-0 output as a position. In the example it predicts 3.75 for key 1, which is at position 0. Stage 0 is graded only on whether it routes keys to leaves that can fit them, not on its own accuracy.

blocks.question: You double the number of leaf models in a 2-stage RMI from 10,000 to 20,000. What happens to the per-lookup work of evaluating models?
options: It stays the same: one stage-0 model and one leaf model per lookup
It roughly doubles, because the top model must compare against twice as many leaves
It grows by one level, like adding a level to a B-tree
It halves, because each leaf covers half as many keys
blocks.explain: Routing is arithmetic: floor(M x f0(x) / N) jumps straight to a leaf, whatever M is. More leaves cost memory and can tighten error windows, which can shorten the final search, but model evaluation stays one model per stage.

blocks.question: Leaf L1 in the example has 9 keys and errors from -1 to +1, while the other leaves have zero error. If you could afford one more leaf model, where should it go?
options: Split L0, because it has the fewest keys
Split L1, because it has the widest error window and covers the most keys
Add it on top as a stage-0 model, to improve routing accuracy
Nowhere: zero-error leaves prove the RMI is already optimal
blocks.explain: Lookups routed to L1 search 3 slots and everyone else searches 1. Splitting L1 into two narrower slices is where extra capacity reduces search work. This is the intuition behind adaptive designs like ALEX and the error-driven segmentation of the PGM-index.

lessons.title: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models

blocks.md: After the model predicts position $p$, the learned index still has to find the record. Kraska et al. store, for every leaf, the worst under- and over-prediction over its keys and search only $[p + \text{min\_err}, p + \text{max\_err}]$. Inside that window they use **model-biased binary search**: an ordinary binary search whose first midpoint is $p$ itself, not the window center. For string keys, where each comparison is expensive, they also tested **biased quaternary search**, which probes $p - \sigma$, $p$ and $p + \sigma$ first ($\sigma$ is the leaf's standard error) so that the CPU can prefetch all three.

The cost of a bounded binary search depends on the *worst* error of the leaf, not on how far off this particular prediction was: a window of $W$ slots costs about $\log_2 W$ probes, whether the key is at $p$ or at the edge. ALEX (Ding et al., SIGMOD 2020) uses **exponential search** instead: probe $p \pm 1, p \pm 2, p \pm 4, \dots$ until the key is bracketed, then binary search inside the last bracket. Its cost grows with the *actual* error $d$ of this lookup, about $2\log_2 d$ probes, and it needs no stored bounds at all.

blocks.title: Probes needed: bounded binary versus exponential search

scenes.caption: Simplified probe-count model (real cost also depends on cache misses). A 4,096-slot window costs 12 probes for every key. Exponential search is cheaper when the actual error is below about 45, a bit under sqrt(4,096) = 64.
A badly fitting leaf with a 2^20-slot worst case: bounded search pays 20 probes on every lookup, even when most predictions are close. Exponential search pays only for the error it actually meets.
A tight leaf with a 16-slot window: bounded search costs 4 probes and exponential search loses as soon as the error exceeds a few slots. Neither strategy wins everywhere.

blocks.md: ALEX reports that, in its experiments, exponential search without bounds was faster than binary search with bounds, because good models put most keys very close to the prediction. The crossover in the figure is the intuition: $1 + 2\log_2 d < \log_2 W$ roughly when $d < \sqrt{W}$.

There is a subtle correctness issue too. The stored bounds come from running the model on the *stored* keys. A range query or an insert asks for the lower_bound of a key that may not be stored. If the model is **monotonic** (a larger key never gets a smaller prediction), an absent key's prediction lies between those of its stored neighbours, so the bounds still hold. If it is not monotonic, which a neural network or an RMI with leaf boundaries can easily be, the true lower_bound of an absent key can lie outside the window.

blocks.prompt: A non-monotonic leaf predicts position 900 for stored key 5,000 and position 880 for an absent key 5,001. Its stored bounds are min_err = -10, max_err = +10. Where can the lower_bound of 5,001 be, and what goes wrong?
blocks.reveal: The lower_bound of 5,001 is the slot right after key 5,000, so it is near 901. The window for 5,001 is 870 to 890, which does not contain it. A plain bounded search returns the edge of the window, a **wrong** answer. The paper lists three fixes: force the model to be monotonic, or detect that the search ended on a window boundary and widen it, or use exponential search, which keeps going until it brackets the key.

blocks.md: Always handle the case where the search lands on the edge of the window. With stored min/max bounds, a hit on the boundary is the signal that a non-monotonic model may have pushed the true answer outside.

Bounded search costs the leaf's worst-case error on every lookup. Exponential search costs the error of this lookup. Tight models favour bounded search; loose models with mostly good predictions favour exponential search.

blocks.question: A leaf has min_err = -2,000 and max_err = +2,000, but 99% of its keys are predicted within 8 slots. Which search strategy is likely faster on average, and why?
options: Exponential search, because its cost follows the typical error (about 8) rather than the 4,001-slot worst case
Bounded binary search, because the window guarantees correctness
Neither: both cost log2 of the array size
Linear scan, because errors are small
blocks.explain: Bounded binary search over 4,001 slots needs about 12 probes for every key. Exponential search with an error of 8 needs about 1 + 2 log2(8) = 7. Since nearly all keys are close, the exponential strategy wins on average, which is the effect ALEX measured.

blocks.question: Spot the bug. A learned index answers range scans by computing p = round(f(lo_key)), then binary searching [p + min_err, p + max_err] and scanning forward from the result. f is a small neural net and the bounds were computed on stored keys. Range scans sometimes miss the first few rows. Why?
options: Binary search is the wrong algorithm; it should be linear
The error bounds should be computed on random keys, not stored keys
lo_key is usually absent, and a non-monotonic f can place its lower_bound outside the stored window
Rounding should be floor, not round
blocks.explain: Bounds from stored keys only guarantee hits for stored keys. A range start is usually not a stored key, and a non-monotonic model can predict it far from its stored neighbours. Widen the search when it ends on a window edge, use exponential search, or use a monotonic model.

lessons.title: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments

blocks.md: The RMI fixes its shape first (stages, models per stage) and measures the errors afterwards, so its error is whatever the data gives. The **PGM-index** (Piecewise Geometric Model index, Ferragina and Vinciguerra, VLDB 2020) turns this around: you choose the maximum error $\varepsilon$ up front, and the structure is built to meet it.

Its building block is an $\varepsilon$-approximate **segment**: a triple (first key, slope, intercept) such that, for every key $k$ it covers, the line's prediction is within $\varepsilon$ of the key's true position. A segment takes constant space (two floats and one key) whether it covers 10 keys or 10 million. A **piecewise linear approximation** (PLA) is a sequence of such segments covering all keys.

blocks.tex: \big|\,\text{slope}\cdot k + \text{intercept} - \operatorname{rank}(k)\,\big| \le \varepsilon \quad \text{for every key } k \text{ in the segment}
blocks.caption: rank(k) is the true position of k in the sorted array. A lookup then searches only 2 epsilon + 1 slots around the prediction.

blocks.md: How many segments are needed? The paper uses a streaming algorithm from time-series compression (O'Rourke, 1981) that computes the **minimum** number of segments in linear time. It adds points (key, position) one at a time while some line still fits all of them within $\varepsilon$; geometrically, while the convex hull of the points fits in a strip of height $2\varepsilon$. When the next point breaks this, it closes the segment and starts a new one.
Here is that process on 24 keys with $\varepsilon = 1$. The keys come in three regimes: a dense run, a second dense run starting at 40, and a sparse tail.

blocks.title: Covering 24 keys with segments of error at most 1

scenes.caption: Twenty-four sorted keys, positions 0 to 23. We want the fewest lines such that every key's predicted position is within 1 of its true position.
Segment s0 grows from key 2 through key 14. Adding key 40 at position 9 would need a jump no line within error 1 can make, so s0 closes after 9 keys.
Segment s1 covers keys 40 to 50, and s2 covers the sparse tail 95 to 310. Three segments cover all 24 keys; the greedy procedure gives the minimum count.
Predictions from one valid line per segment, rounded. In the tail, keys 95, 160 and 200 are off by 1 after rounding; their unrounded errors (-0.62, +0.75, +0.74) stay inside the limit of 1.

blocks.md: The segment lines used here, as (first key, slope, intercept) with the line evaluated at key minus first key, are s0 = (2, 0.6629, 0.129), s1 = (40, 0.6771, 9.115) and s2 = (95, 0.0251, 17.622). A useful bound follows from the definition: any $2\varepsilon$ consecutive keys can be covered by the flat line through the middle of their positions, so every segment in the optimal PLA covers at least $2\varepsilon$ keys and the number of segments $m$ obeys:

blocks.caption: Lemma 2 of the PGM paper. In practice, when the data is regular, m is far smaller than this bound.

blocks.md: Now the recursion that makes it a *pure* learned index. Take the first key of every segment (here 2, 40 and 95), treat them as a new sorted array, and build an optimal PLA over them with the same $\varepsilon$. Repeat until one segment remains: that segment is the root. Because each level shrinks the count by a factor of at least $2\varepsilon$, there are $O(\log_{2\varepsilon} m)$ levels, and each level costs one multiply-add plus a binary search over $2\varepsilon + 1$ slots. No B-tree is needed anywhere, unlike the FITing-tree (which indexes its segments with a B+tree) or the RMI's hybrid fallback.

blocks.title: A two-level PGM-index looking up key 44

scenes.caption: Each node is one segment. The root's segment indexes the first keys of the level below, exactly as a leaf segment indexes the data.
Root: 0.0218 x (44 - 2) - 0.138 = 0.78, rounded to 1. Search slots 0 to 2 of the level below for the last first-key <= 44: that is 40, so go to s1.
s1: 0.6771 x (44 - 40) + 9.115 = 11.82, rounded to 12. Binary search positions 11 to 13 (2 epsilon + 1 = 3 slots) and find 44 at position 12.

blocks.md: How small does this get on bigger data? Below are segment counts from the same greedy algorithm on 400,000 synthetic 64-bit keys, one set drawn from a log-normal distribution ($\mu = 0, \sigma = 2$, the shape of the RMI paper's synthetic dataset) and one drawn uniformly at random. The bound $n / 2\varepsilon$ would allow 3,125 segments at $\varepsilon = 64$.

blocks.title: Optimal segments for 400,000 keys as epsilon grows

scenes.caption: Log-normal keys: 1,521 segments at eps 8 but only 72 at eps 64. At 24 bytes per segment, 72 segments take 1,728 bytes, about 29 times less than a sparse index storing one 16-byte entry per 128-key page (50,000 bytes).
Uniform random keys: 1,488 segments at eps 8 even though the distribution is a straight line. Random gaps make positions wander by more than 8 slots at small scale. At eps 512 one segment suffices.

blocks.md: A close relative, **RadixSpline** (Kipf et al., 2020), is built the same bottom-up way in a single pass: an error-bounded spline over the data, plus a flat *radix table* indexed by the top $r$ bits of the key that tells which spline points to binary search. It has just two parameters, the error bound and $r$.

Pick epsilon, get a guarantee. The PGM-index fixes the last-mile search to 2 epsilon + 1 slots per level, uses the fewest segments that can meet that bound, and so its space adapts to how regular the data is.

Fewer levels is not automatically faster. The SOSD benchmark study (Marcus et al., 2020) found cache misses were the single most explanatory performance counter: each PGM level likely costs a cache miss, so a large RMI with a low error can beat a PGM-index of similar error, while an RMI that cannot get its error down loses that edge.

blocks.question: You halve epsilon in a PGM-index over the same data. What do you expect?
options: Fewer segments and a faster last-mile search
More segments (more memory), a smaller search window per level, and possibly more levels
The same number of segments, because the optimal PLA does not depend on epsilon
Lookups become approximate
blocks.explain: A tighter error bound means each line covers fewer keys, so m grows (the bars show 72 segments at eps 64 versus 139 at eps 32 for log-normal keys). Each level's search window shrinks to 2 epsilon + 1, and the fan-out per level, at least 2 epsilon, shrinks too, so the tree can get deeper.

blocks.question: Why can uniform random keys need about as many segments as log-normal keys at epsilon 8?
options: The greedy algorithm is not optimal for uniform data
Uniform keys have duplicates
Linear models cannot represent a uniform CDF
At small scale, random gaps make the positions deviate from any line by more than 8 slots, so the distribution's global shape barely matters
blocks.explain: The uniform CDF is a straight line globally, but the actual positions of random keys wander around that line, and over 400,000 keys those excursions exceed 8 slots often. With a larger epsilon the wiggles fit inside the band and uniform data collapses to a single segment at eps 512. Model the data you have, not the distribution it came from.

lessons.title: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off

blocks.md: Everything so far assumed a read-only array. Inserting into a sorted dense array means shifting every later record, and new keys can shift the CDF so that stored error bounds stop holding. The original paper lists write-heavy workloads as an open challenge. Two answers have emerged: make the structure updatable, or rebuild it whenever the data is rewritten anyway.

**ALEX** (Ding et al., SIGMOD 2020) takes the first path. Its leaves, called data nodes, each hold a linear model and a **Gapped Array**: an array with free slots spread between keys instead of only at the end as in a B+tree leaf. Keys are placed by **model-based insertion**, at the slot the model predicts, so lookups usually land right on the key. Gaps absorb inserts without large shifts, and a bitmap records which slots hold keys so that scans skip gaps.

A worked example. A data node holds 6 keys at ALEX's default lower density limit $d_l = 0.6$, the density a node has right after an expansion (bulk load uses 0.7), so it has $6 / 0.6 = 10$ slots. The model is a least-squares line on (key, rank), scaled from 6 positions to 10 slots: slot $= \lfloor 0.1654k - 1.0696 \rfloor$. Each key goes to its predicted slot, or to the next free one to the right if that is taken.

blocks.title: A Gapped Array absorbing two inserts

scenes.caption: Model-based placement: 12, 15 and 21 predict slots 0, 1 and 2; 40 predicts 5.54 (slot 5), 44 predicts 6.21 (slot 6) and 58 predicts 8.52 (slot 8). Gaps (_) are left where the model expects no keys. Density is 6/10.
Insert 50: the model predicts 7.20, slot 7. It is a gap between 44 and 58, so 50 drops in with no shifting. Density 7/10.

Insert 42: it predicts slot 5, held by 40, and 42 must sit between 40 and 44 with no gap there. ALEX shifts toward the nearest gap: 40 moves left to slot 4, and 42 takes slot 5. One move, not a shift of the whole tail.

Density is now 8/10 = 0.8, the default upper limit d_u. The next insert first expands the node to 8 / 0.6, about 13 slots, re-placing every key with a rescaled or retrained model. Meanwhile 40 sits one slot left of its prediction; exponential search finds it.

blocks.md: ALEX also keeps per-node cost models (average log2 prediction error for lookups, average distance to the nearest gap for inserts). When a node is full and its observed cost has drifted from what was expected, which happens when inserted keys do not follow the old distribution, it may split the node sideways or downward instead of expanding it. On its benchmarks the paper reports up to 4.1 times the throughput of a B+tree across read-write workloads, never worse, with up to 2000 times smaller index size.

The second path suits the LSM trees from your prerequisite course. Their SSTable files are immutable and written in sorted order during flushes and compactions, which is exactly when a one-pass learned index can be trained for almost no extra cost. The RadixSpline paper makes exactly this argument: the merge already produces sorted data, so training adds only a small constant overhead.

The clearest production story is Google's **Bigtable** (Abu-Libdeh et al., 2020). Bigtable's SSTables used a two-level block index; a cache miss on an index block costs an extra read from the distributed file system. The team trained a linear model on string keys (converted to integers with a per-character base) to predict *byte offset*, then **chose the block boundaries to match the model**: record $k$ goes to block $\lfloor f(k) / \tau \rfloor$, where $\tau$ is the target block size. Because the data layout follows the model, the predicted block is always right, and no keys are stored in the index.

blocks.title: Bigtable SSTable lookup: block index versus learned index

scenes.caption: Default path: the in-memory level-0 index points to level-1 index blocks, which are loaded when needed. With a cold or crowded cache, a lookup can cost an index-block read before the data-block read.
Learned path: one multiply-add gives a block number and an array gives its disk location. The index is tiny, so it stays in memory and no index block has to be fetched.

Reported gains on 256M rows of 1 KB with random integer keys: mean latency down 36% for point lookups and 22% for scans; mean throughput up 55% and 28%. They come from fewer block reads, not from faster arithmetic.

blocks.md: Bigtable's lesson: if you control the layout, make the data follow the model instead of making the model follow the data. Then the prediction is never wrong and there is no last-mile search across blocks.

When does a learned index pay off? The original paper's own numbers show how much depends on the data. It compared a 2-stage RMI to a read-optimized B-tree with 128 keys per page (its fastest setting, about 13 MB) on datasets of about 200M keys each:

blocks.title: Lookup time (ns) from Kraska et al., Figure 4

scenes.caption: Maps (longitudes of about 200M map features), a fairly linear CDF: 98 ns with 10k leaves versus 265 ns for the B-tree, with a 0.15 MB index instead of 13.11 MB.

Weblogs (request timestamps shaped by class schedules, weekends and holidays), which the authors call almost a worst case: 10k leaves only reach 222 ns, and it takes 200k leaves (3.05 MB) to reach 126 ns.
Synthetic log-normal keys, a heavy tail: 178 ns at 10k leaves, improving to 146 ns at 200k. Every RMI here is still smaller than the B-tree.

blocks.md: Treat the headline speedups as conditional. They were measured on in-memory, read-only, sorted integer keys. String keys (only up to 1.12 times faster in the same paper), heavy insert traffic, adversarial key sets and distribution shift all erode the gains, and a well-tuned traditional baseline matters: the SOSD benchmark was built to answer skepticism about comparisons against strong implementations.

blocks.question: Your service stores immutable sorted files that are rewritten by background compaction, and lookups are read-heavy. Which learned index design fits most naturally?
options: An ALEX-style updatable index, because data changes over time
A one-pass, error-bounded index (RadixSpline or PGM-style) rebuilt during each compaction
A single deep neural network trained once and never retrained
None: learned indexes cannot be used with files on disk
blocks.explain: Each file is written once in sorted order and then never modified, so the model never goes stale for that file. A single-pass build during the merge costs little extra, which is exactly the argument the RadixSpline paper makes for LSM trees.

blocks.question: In Bigtable's design a weak model makes some blocks much larger than the target size tau. What breaks?
options: Lookups return wrong rows
Range scans stop working because the model is not monotonic
Nothing is incorrect; block sizes just become uneven, which can cost some read efficiency
Every lookup must now search neighbouring blocks
blocks.explain: Records are assigned to block floor(f(k) / tau) by the model itself, so the predicted block is correct by construction. A monotonic f keeps keys sorted so scans still work. A poor fit only makes block sizes less uniform.

blocks.question: A table's keys are inserted in an order whose distribution differs sharply from the keys already loaded. In ALEX, what is the main risk and the built-in response?
options: The model becomes inaccurate, leaving long runs with no gaps; ALEX detects the cost drift and splits or retrains nodes
Keys are lost because model-based insertion overwrites slots
Deletes slow down because they must shift keys
Nothing, because exponential search makes model accuracy irrelevant
blocks.explain: Model-based insertion depends on the model; if new keys do not follow it, they pile up and create long contiguous runs where every insert shifts many keys and searches go further. ALEX compares observed cost with the expected cost from its cost models and then expands with retraining or splits the node.
